title: Ines and the Atlas
premise: In 1913, Rosalind Ravensworth drives for the formidable suffragist Lady Edith Vane, reading every letter she carries and keeping her own past sealed tight. When a gaunt stranger named Ines arrives bearing a letter in the unmistakable hand of Lord Ashcombe—a man publicly drowned two years ago—Rosalind realizes the 'corpse' has been alive, hiding, and writing to someone dangerous. The letter is proof of a conspiracy between shipping magnates and government officials to sink a vessel for insurance, blaming striking dockworkers. To expose it before the evidence is destroyed aboard the Atlas, Rosalind and Ines must smuggle the letter through three checkpoints—customs, the docks police, and the ship itself—and get it into the hands of a journalist before the morning tide. They succeed at terrible cost: Ines takes a bullet meant for the letter, survives, and finds in Rosalind and Lady Vane's household the family she never had, while Rosalind finally stops being invisible.
about_author: Tamsin Thornbury is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing Edwardian suffrage papers in Yorkshire. She writes historical fiction about the women history filed under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Letters I Should Not Read
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. We meet her routine: driving Lady Vane through Leeds, memorizing letters she officially never opens, and keeping her own history locked away. Emotional beat: competent loneliness—the comfort and cost of invisibility.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Service Door
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. A rain-soaked woman appears at the kitchen door asking for 'the lady who fights,' clutching an oilskin packet. Rosalind nearly turns her away until she glimpses the handwriting inside. Beat: wary curiosity sparking against instinct.

chapters.title: The Hand of a Drowned Man
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She compares the letter to archived correspondence and confirms it matches Lord Ashcombe, dead these two years. Lady Vane reads it and goes very still. Beat: dread—the world tilts from ordinary to lethal.

chapters.title: What the Atlas Carries
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. She explains how she came by the letter: her brother was a clerk aboard the Atlas and died in its 'accidental' sinking; this letter proves the sinking was arranged. Beat: grief transmuted into purpose.

chapters.title: Lady Vane Decides
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Lady Vane weighs the risk to the movement against the injustice, then commits: the letter must reach journalist Nathaniel Quill in Southampton before the Atlas sails on Thursday's tide. Beat: resolve hardening into a plan.

chapters.title: Packing for Two
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The women prepare disguises and cover stories—Rosalind as a chauffeuse delivering motor parts, Ines as her sister. Small domestic scenes of trust forming. Beat: tentative warmth, the first stitches of found family.

chapters.title: Checkpoint One: Customs House
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. At Leeds customs, a sharp-eyed inspector detains them over forged manifests. Rosalind bluffs using knowledge gleaned from years of read letters. Beat: terror mastered by skill; they pass by inches.

chapters.title: Night Train South
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. On the overnight train, the two trade life stories; Ines reveals she recognized Rosalind's name from her brother's papers. Betrayal or bond? Beat: intimacy shadowed by suspicion.

chapters.title: The Man in the Bowler Hat
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A watcher follows them from London; Rosalind executes a switch through King's Cross crowds, but realizes he knew her face—not Ines's. Someone from her hidden past is hunting. Beat: her secret begins to crack open.

chapters.title: Rosalind's Other Name
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Cornered in a boarding house, Rosalind confesses: she is the daughter of one of the conspirators, who faked her death after she threatened to expose him years ago. Beat: shame met with unexpected grace.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Two: The Dock Police
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Southampton dock police, tipped off, search every vehicle. Lady Vane arrives unexpectedly as distraction, deploying fame like a weapon while the letter passes in a spare tyre. Beat: exhilaration of allies in concert.

chapters.title: Quill Refuses
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Journalist Nathaniel Quill, warned off by his editor, refuses to print without corroboration. The letter alone isn't enough—they need testimony or the ship's manifest. Beat: despair; the plan's foundation crumbles.

chapters.title: Aboard the Atlas
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. They secure passage as hired drivers for a first-class passenger, boarding the ship that killed Ines's brother. Beat: awe and horror walking the same decks.

chapters.title: The Captain's Cabin
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Searching for the manifest, Ines comes face to face with the man who signed her brother's death order—alive, respectable, ashore for the night. She nearly kills him. Beat: rage against the edge of ruin.

chapters.title: Caught Between Tides
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The bowler-hat man boards; Rosalind is recognized and detained below decks as the ship prepares to sail. Beat: claustrophobic fear—trapped with the truth and no way out.

chapters.title: Ines Alone
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. With Rosalind captive and dawn approaching, Ines must choose: flee with the letter or go back for her. She hides the letter in the one place no one will search and returns. Beat: love outweighing survival.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Three: The Gangway
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. At the gangway, guards check every leaving passenger. Ines creates chaos—loosed cargo, a staged fainting fit—and Rosalind slips free as the tide turns. Beat: desperate, breathless escape.

chapters.title: The Morning Tide
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The Atlas sails without the evidence, but the letter reaches Quill via Lady Vane's arranged courier, corroborated by the manifest pages Ines tore free. Beat: exhausted triumph shadowed by what it cost.

chapters.title: Reckoning
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The story breaks; arrests follow; Rosalind confronts her father across an interview-room table and walks away without hatred. Beat: release—power exposed cannot corrupt quietly anymore.

chapters.title: What Ines Buried
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines visits her brother's grave with news he can finally rest beneath, and admits she stayed not for vengeance but because someone asked her to stay. Beat: mourning turning toward belonging.

chapters.title: The Household of Ravensworth
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Back in Leeds, the household absorbs Ines permanently—Lady Vane declares her secretary, Rosalind declares her family. Beat: quiet joy; the found family made official.

chapters.title: Letters Worth Reading
chapters.summary: Shared POV. Months later, Rosalind hands Ines a letter unopened—an act of total trust—and together they write their own account for the archive. Beat: resolution; invisibility traded, willingly, for witness.
